items.title: Toward an Indigenous Curatorial Practice: Learning From Tłıchǫ Metaphors of Care to Establish Principles of Curation
items.affiliation: Western University; Government of Northwest Territories

extra.summary: ABSTRACT The displacement of items of cultural heritage from Indigenous communities is continually perpetuated through their appropriation into collection systems that are inappropriate to Indigenous laws and customs. This paper presents the efforts of the Tłı̨chǫ Government (TG) to address such issues by creating a system that is rooted within its values and traditions for the curation of its cultural heritage. It is embarking on this journey through the creation of its digital archive and the development of programming for its community museum in Behchokǫ̀, Northwest Territories (NWT), Canada. This process first entailed stepping back to carefully consider Tłı̨chǫ traditions of caring for knowledge and cultural heritage through learning circles and a Strong like Two methodology. Analyses of these results were then used to infer principles of curation—ownership, preservation, stewardship, and categorization. This research contributes to the decolonization of the field of cultural heritage management (CHM) and presents a leading example of how the exercise of sovereignty over cultural heritage by Indigenous Nations stands to reactivate displaced belongings within their communities.

items.title: Spectral Ecologies: Sintering More‐Than‐Human Pasts to Less‐Than‐Certain Futures

extra.summary: ABSTRACT How do we mourn the loss of more‐than‐human beings, and what becomes of them when they are gone? This commentary examines two installations in Spectral Remix , an art exhibition at the 2025 American Anthropological Association Annual Meeting in New Orleans. The first is Cymene Howe and Dominic Boyer's Glacier Graveyard , which memorializes glaciers lost to anthropogenic climate change. The second is the XYZ Collective's The Atlas of Heritage Trees , which uses laser scanning, 3D printing, and digital animation to rematerialize ancient trees now threatened by climate change and saltwater intrusion. Drawing on embodied and affective encounters with each installation, I show how Glacier Graveyard extends human funerary rituals to glaciers through an immersive and visceral encounter, while The Atlas of Heritage Trees imagines uncanny technoscientific afterlives for dying trees as they are translated into digital forms. I engage the analytic of sintering —which refers to both the physical process that bonds ephemeral snowflakes into durable glacial ice and an advanced laser technique used in 3D printing—to examine uncanny resonances across these two more‐than‐human works. Taken together, these works show how installation as a medium can facilitate a deeper reckoning with more‐than‐human pasts and less‐than‐certain futures, forcing us to confront which bonds we choose to make and which bonds we choose to break in our shared worlds.

items.title: Spectral Remix: A Group Commentary on a Group Installation
Becoming climate sentinels
items.affiliation: Victoria University of Wellington; Victoria University

extra.summary: Abstract In South Korea, forest scientists refashion themselves as “climate sentinels” as they confront subtle yet disquieting shifts in plant seasonality brought about by climate change. Unlike traditional sentinels, who watch for external threats from a frontier, climate sentinels face ecological anomalies and surprises—such as untimely flowering—that have permeated everyday spaces. To register such ecological perplexities, they engage in technoscientific entrainments: deliberate, disciplinary, and laborious coordinations of human observers, trees, protocols, institutions, and modular devices into a shared rhythm of attention. These experimental processes redistribute the traditional embodied technique of mokch’ŭk (eye observation) across nationwide phenological observation networks while reanimating the ecological significance of plant seasonality. For these sentinels, confronting climate change requires attending not only to satellites and heavily computed models but also to the distributed, more‐than‐human experiments through which ecological perplexities are made sensible on the ground.

extra.summary: Abstract An anthropology of horror can serve as a vernacular critique of financial speculation. Drawing on fieldwork in San Pedro, Paraguay, I track horror across three registers: pombero tricksters; plata yvyguy (buried money) as a founding myth of postwar finance; and obligations binding sesame farmers to monsters, patrones , and creditors. Horror—a critical ontology and distinctive wonder—arises when obligation becomes undecidable: when one cannot tell whether the forces manipulating time and the future are persons who stand in relation, or how far the liability extends. Paraguay has produced this condition twice, first under the Stroessner dictatorship (1954–89), with its network of civilian informants, and later under climate finance running through the same clientelist orders. As Martha Blache's 1982 study of Guarani folklore helps us understand, finance bears rather than subsumes the moral arrangements of prestation, and horror is a native theorization of speculation rather than a response to an external capitalist threat.

items.title: The power of reflexivity and the uneasiness it provokes
The politics of evidence making
items.affiliation: Victoria University of Wellington; New Zealand Law Society; Emory University; University of Auckland

extra.summary: Abstract What is evidence, and how is it constituted across different scientific, legal, political and social domains? Courts, medical clinics, scientific enterprises, public constituencies, as well as academic journals, come to define, adjudicate, and thus constitute evidence through a variety of openly and covertly political processes, as Sameena Mulla and Courtney Addison discuss. Reflecting on fieldwork they have conducted on a range of topics—including sexual assault intervention, forensic evidence collection, court sentencing, genomic medicine, and conservation—they suggest what kinds of questions anthropologists might want to ask in thinking through not only the nature of evidence making but also its impact on social communities. They also highlight what is at stake in the shaping and contestation of evidence, including justice, social cohesion and environmental futures.

items.title: Reassessment of the morphological evidence for hominin hybrids in the Levant
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute
items.affiliation: University College London; University of Reading; Natural History Museum

extra.summary: The Levantine hominin fossil and archaeological records have played a central role in long‐standing palaeoanthropological debates over origin models and possible interbreeding between Neanderthals ( Homo neanderthalensis ) and Homo sapiens . Recent research has provided a strong framework for the morphological expectations of recent hybrid ancestry in primates, along with renewed suggestions that early Late Pleistocene hominins from the Levant show morphological evidence of hybridization. Here we address these developments by using established diagnostic features of H. sapiens and H. neanderthalensis to review possible fossil evidence of hybridization from the key Levantine sites of Qafzeh, Skhūl, and Tabūn. We conclude that, while individuals from these sites show a perplexing combination of characteristics that broadly overlap with expectations of hybridization, this explanation can only be established once other alternatives have been ruled out, or through the recovery of genetic material from these key fossils.

extra.summary: Lauren Benton reminds us that to write about piracy as historians (and anthropologists) is to engage in projects of “myth-making and myth-busting.” As she notes, pirates are either imagined as “colorful rogues…inherently anti-authoritarian actors who possessed a penchant for experimenting with alternative forms of political solidarity,” or they are depicted in a less renegade fashion, one that shows “their integration in established, if fluid, networks of patronage and power.” Instead of colorful outlaws, Benton (2014) argues that pirates are more akin to lawyers engaged in “legal posturing,” converting “booty into property.” As political actors, their politics are often far from revolutionary. items.title: Ibn Khaldûn as a Colonial Archive: Toward an Epistemic Decolonization
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract This article examines Ibn Khaldûn not as a stable, timeless precursor of modern social science but as a figure constituted through colonial translation and reception. Focusing on nineteenth- and twentieth-century French and English translations of the Muqaddimah , it argues that Ibn Khaldûn emerged in modern scholarship as a colonial archive—a site where translation, race, and epistemic authority intersected to produce new forms of historical and sociological knowledge. Through close comparison of Arabic originals and their European translations, the article shows how colonial epistemologies reconfigured Ibn Khaldûn’s analytical categories—particularly those concerning tribe, generation, civilization, and climate—into racialized frameworks foreign to his medieval context. It further demonstrates how this translated Ibn Khaldûn became selectively relevant to European social science while remaining excluded from its canonical genealogies. Finally, the article critically reassesses the enduring claim that Ibn Khaldûn articulated racist views about Black populations, showing that this attribution itself belongs to the colonial archive generated through translation rather than to the epistemic logic of the original text. The article thus contributes to comparative histories of knowledge, colonial epistemology, and the global formation of the social sciences.

items.title: Borrowed Time: Sovereign Debt and Temporal Disorder In Socialist Yugoslavia
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract When Francis Fukuyama described the collapse of state socialism as marking the “end of history,” he captured the imagination of the post-Cold War moment, rendering the fall of the Berlin Wall a metonym for the definitive eclipse of communism and the advent of a new era of liberal capitalist hegemony. For Europe’s Left, the term became associated with a moment of profound demoralization. Fukuyama’s end of history, however, was only one moment of a longer and more expansive crisis in the socialist order of time. This crisis can be traced back to the global economic upheavals of the 1970s that impacted both social democracy in the West and state socialism in the East. A decade before crowds forced their way across a divided Berlin, socialism on both sides of the Iron Curtain had entered an existential decline. This article argues that the sovereign debt crises that beset European states in the final decade of the Cold War disrupted socialism’s regime of historicity. It develops this argument with reference to late-socialist Yugoslavia and demonstrates how the temporal conditions of sovereign indebtedness shaped popular culture. Through a reading of the films Balkanski špijun (1984) and Već viđeno (1987), the article argues that the erosion of socialism’s horizons of expectation fostered a new experience of historical time in which the past returned in uncanny, troubling, and ultimately destructive ways.

items.title: The paradox of violent sanctuary: rethinking the concept of sanctuary in protracted refugee camp contexts

extra.summary: Refugee camps have been depicted as spaces that adversely affect refugees by, among other things, exposing them to psychosocial problems, violence, exploitation, and material deprivation. In Kakuma, the prevalence of violence inside and around the camp, which involves serious injuries, is high. Yet, with all its challenges, the camp is a near-cosmopolitan site where multiple cultures interact, generate livelihoods, and find protection from conflicts and hardships that forced their displacement. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork conducted in 2023 in Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp, this article challenges that binary by developing the concept of a violent sanctuary to explain the camp’s paradoxical character. It argues that the camp simultaneously offers refuge from external violence and generates new forms of struggle within its boundaries. This article makes a theoretical as well as empirical contribution by extending sanctuary scholarship into camp studies and showing how sanctuary can be understood as a relational and uneven condition.

extra.summary: This article examines how Berlin's Kurdish diaspora and diaspora-centric Kurdistan's Jews in Jerusalem embrace music performances to meet their cultural, political, and social affairs. Comparing culturally and historically connected yet politically and socially distinct dispersed populations, it argues that music performances constitute not only cultural and symbolic expressions but also wide-ranging mechanisms of cultural self-organisation among diasporic populations to express, transmit, and represent group identities and political agendas. Based on ethnographic field research, including 87 in-depth interviews and participant observations, the article explores how individual singers, music bands, cultural associations, and religious institutions perform and facilitate music to impact diasporic life. The findings suggest that Kurdish music performances in Berlin are largely intertwined with homeland-oriented political aspirations, whereas the music production in Jerusalem is treated as ancestral heritage to evoke collective memories, shaping and preserving group identities. extra.summary: As motherhood extends from the private sphere to the public arena of social media, it can no longer be understood merely as a form of social division of labour. items.title: Immigration for realists: how we misread the public and the evidence, and how to do better
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Immigration experts have never known more, and rarely mattered less. Restrictionist parties and arguments have become increasingly influential across immigrant-receiving democracies, even as the expert consensus on immigration's benefits has grown more confident. I argue that we, immigration scholars and practitioners, have ourselves contributed to this gap. First, we misread the public: most voters are neither committed xenophobes nor dormant cosmopolitans. Rather, they are conditional supporters willing to accept immigration they see as beneficial to their country. Their underlying preferences are strikingly stable, with opponents usually caring more about the issue than supporters. Second, we misrepresent the evidence on immigration's costs and benefits through selective framing and strategic omission. While the effects of freer human mobility are generally positive, these findings come with qualifications that experts often leave out. Voters who notice a mismatch with their experience have good reason to distrust us, which damages the case for immigration regardless of what the populist far right does. I argue for an immigration realism that takes voters' preferences seriously and reports inconvenient evidence as readily as favourable evidence. Instead of trying to change opponents' minds, we should put more effort into designing demonstrably beneficial policy compromises that can retain majority support.

items.title: A pool of living water: managed circulation and migrant suspension along the China–Myanmar border
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Contemporary migration regimes often admit migrants into labour markets while withholding full social and legal incorporation. Building on this insight, this article introduces the concept of managed circulation to capture a compressed temporal configuration of inclusion and exclusion, in which admission and potential removal are organised within the same governing framework and often within a remarkably short time horizon. Drawing on ethnographic research among Myanmar migrants at the China–Myanmar border, this research shows how mobility is governed through administrative temporal windows defined by the validity and renewal requirements of border passes. Migrants are recruited into local labour markets while simultaneously remaining vulnerable to document expiration and repatriation. The article further develops the concept of migrant suspension to describe the lived condition produced by managed circulation. Temporal urgency embedded in managed circulation compels repeated, often involuntary movement as migrants seek to maintain legal presence and secure livelihoods. By examining two distinct temporal windows and migrants’ strategies for navigating them, the article demonstrates how mobility itself becomes a condition of suspension rather than incorporation. It also argues that Myanmar border-pass holders constitute a significant and enduring component of China’s cross-border labour regime rather than an exception to it.

extra.summary: This article discusses the inventory efforts of the Keratuan Darah Putih heritage as a strategic step in preserving the collective memory of the indigenous Lampung community. Keratuan Darah Putih is one of the oldest customary kingdoms in Lampung, rich in historical, cultural, and spiritual values. Unfortunately, many of its historical legacies ranging from buildings and ancient manuscripts to oral traditions remain undocumented and are experiencing a decline in significance due to a lack of youth interest and the pressures of modernization. This study employs a qualitative approach through in-depth interviews with traditional leaders, royal descendants, and local community members. The findings reveal that the kingdom's heritage serves not only as a symbol of identity but also as a medium for sustaining collective memory and the transmission of noble values within Lampung society. Inventory efforts are crucial not only for cultural preservation but also for social restoration and the reinforcement of an authentic local historical narrative. Therefore, a synergistic collaboration between indigenous communities, scholars, and government bodies is essential to develop a participatory-based cultural heritage database that ensures the sustainability of this collective memory across generations.

items.title: Bridging Policy and Practice: Implementing Culturally Responsive Pedagogy in an Ethnically Diverse Primary School in Yunnan, China

extra.summary: This study examines the policy–practice nexus in implementing Culturally Responsive Pedagogy (CRP) in an ethnically diverse primary school in Yunnan Province, China. Through policy document analysis, interviews with eight educators (including the principal), and 20 classroom observations, we identify systemic gaps between provincial CRP policies (e.g., bilingual mandates, cultural curriculum, teacher training) and their enactment. Key barriers include rigid curriculum scheduling, resource shortages (e.g., lack of bilingual materials and trained teachers), and decontextualized professional development. While policies rhetorically endorse CRP, classroom practices remain episodic and symbolic, failing to structurally integrate minority cultures. Nevertheless, teacher-initiated adaptations, such as glossing Chinese vocabulary in Wa and embedding cultural artifacts (e.g., Kongming lanterns) into science instruction, measurably raised student engagement, suggesting that even bounded, episodic responsiveness can yield instructional gains within structural constraints. Drawing on James A. Banks’ Transformation Approach, we argue for systemic reforms: flexible curriculum frameworks, targeted resource allocation, and community-embedded teacher training. The study underscores the need to shift from additive cultural inclusion to transformative pedagogical redesign to achieve equity in Yunnan’s ethnically diverse context.

items.title: Corporate Social Responsibility Fulfillment on the Performance of Chinese Enterprises Overseas: An Empirical Study
items.source: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In increasingly complex international business environments, how multinational enterprises use corporate social responsibility (CSR) to gain host‐country legitimacy and improve performance has become an important issue in international business and CSR research. Drawing on stakeholder theory and the 2018 Overseas Chinese Enterprises and Employees Survey (OCEES) conducted by Yunnan University, this study distinguishes external CSR from internal CSR and examines their differential performance effects, mechanisms, and boundary conditions among overseas Chinese enterprises. The results show that external CSR significantly improves firm performance, mainly through enhanced corporate reputation and pricing capability. In contrast, internal CSR has a less stable performance effect and does not generate the expected positive mechanisms through employee job satisfaction and engagement. Heterogeneity analyses show that external CSR returns are stronger for firms primarily serving host‐country markets and for those operating in low‐income host countries or countries with lower institutional quality than China. Further analysis indicates that, under CSR resource constraints, increasing the share of external CSR in the overall CSR portfolio improves firm performance.

items.title: Beyond Resource Transfer: The Action Logic and Innovative Patterns of Counterpart Assistance for Rural Revitalization in Western China
items.affiliation: Guilin University of Technology; Beihang University

extra.summary: Regional inequality remains a persistent challenge for development governance. When external support is disconnected from local conditions or excessively displaces local actors, resource inputs may fail to generate sustainable development and even weaken local agency. To examine how external support can be transformed into sustainable local capacity, this study integrates neo-endogenous development theory with synergetics to develop an “exogenous–endogenous synergy” framework. Drawing on multiple rounds of fieldwork and interviews, the study finds that Guangdong–Guangxi collaboration has shifted from compensatory resource transfer towards capacity building and institutional embedding. This transformation operates through three interrelated mechanisms: coordinated guidance, multidimensional incentives, and digital empowerment. Variations in local resource endowments and ideational capacity give rise to three context-contingent pathways: integrated advancement, ideational activation, and resource mobilization, each representing a pathway towards an ideal-type model. The findings suggest that cross-regional collaboration may reduce regional inequality when transferred resources are converted into sustainable local capacity, thereby strengthening rather than substituting for local agency.

items.title: Under-platformization: platform literacy and the interplay between multiple actors in developing rural e-commerce in Central and Western China

extra.summary: Abstract Rural e-commerce in China’s central and western regions is often framed as a scalable pathway to rural revitalization. Yet, platformization may also stall, even when there is already a profitable rural industry. Drawing on interviews, fieldwork, and local archives, we examine the Bai silver handicraft cluster in Xinhua Village, Yunnan Province, which despite being a nationally recognized Taobao village, still exhibits under-platformization. We develop a multi-actor framework of platform literacy to explain how platform firms, local governments, aspiring rural e-commerce sellers, and incumbent business elites encounter distinct literacy gaps and misaligned incentives. For high-value craft sectors, category rules, quality verification, and dispute resolution raise market thresholds, while shifting platform rules and uneven local coordination weaken the provision and diffusion of platform know-how. The findings show that under-platformization reflects failures to institutionalize and spread platform literacy across the industry ecosystem, rather than simple technology resistance or a training deficit. These findings offer sector- and governance-sensitive implications for rural digital development.

items.source: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences

extra.summary: Organisational culture is widely recognised as a key factor influencing organisational effectiveness, employee behaviour, and institutional development. items.title: From Temporal Ecstasis to Eternal Wandering: A Zhuangzian Hermeneutic of the Phenomenological Ontological Turn
items.affiliation: Wuhan College; Huazhong University of Science and Technology

extra.summary: This paper employs Zhuangzi’s concept of Xiaoyao (free and easy wandering) as a hermeneutic lens—an interpretive instrument rather than a claim of philosophical correspondence—to re-examine the phenomenological “ontological turn” from Edmund Husserl to Martin Heidegger as a debate fundamentally about temporal ontology. Based on textual evidence drawn primarily from the Inner Chapters of the Zhuangzi, the study reconstructs three experiential-ontological levels in the path toward Xiaoyao: breaking free from the shackles of external things, overcoming the prejudiced mind (Cheng Xin), and achieving selfless merging with nature. This reconstructed path exhibits a formal, heuristic resonance with the three stages of Husserl’s phenomenological reduction, yet their ultimate destinations diverge decisively on the conceptualization of time. Whereas Husserl constitutively reduces “yesterday” and “tomorrow” to intentional modifications of an epistemologically enclosed living present, and Heidegger grounds authenticity in anxiety before finite temporality, Zhuangzi dissolves the linear binary of past and future in the transformation of things (Wu Hua), attaining a non-linear temporal ontology. Acknowledging the internal paradox of willing non-willing, the study shows that Zhuangzi’s freedom is not the absence of struggle but its transformation into tranquility amidst turbulence (Ying Ning)—a phenomenology of liberty fundamentally distinct from the Western phenomenologies of being. items.title: Ethnography Is Contemporary History

extra.summary: The claim that “ethnography is contemporary history” is often dismissed as a truism. Yet this seemingly obvious proposition has been profoundly destabilized by postmodern critiques that expose ethnography’s inherent “fabrication”—its poetics and politics. This article argues that acknowledging such fabrication does not invalidate but rather enriches ethnography’s status as contemporary history. I trace ethnography’s evolution through three eras—amateur, scientific, and reflexive—and engage with canonical works from Malinowski to Fei Xiaotong alongside contemporary innovations such as multi-sited, digital, and multispecies ethnography. I demonstrate that every ethnographic text, precisely through its situated production and perspectival honesty, constitutes an irreplaceable form of contemporary history. The Writing Culture critique, I contend, ultimately reveals not ethnography’s disqualification from historical knowledge but the deeper truth that all historical knowledge is perspectival. By rendering its own perspectives visible, ethnography offers a more honest—and therefore more valuable—mode of contemporary history writing.

items.title: Feminist anthropologies in the contemporary world: A conversation on theory, praxis, and politics
items.affiliation: University of Pittsburgh; Northern Arizona University; Moravian University; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

extra.summary: Abstract This article brings together the voices of members of three major feminist anthropological associations to discuss the state of feminist anthropology as a distinct subfield of anthropology, as well as its state of affairs as an increasingly expanding, as well as increasingly threatened, approach to anthropological theory and praxis worldwide. Composed as a conversation, it is based on a roundtable discussion that took place at the 2022 American Anthropological Association (AAA) Annual Meeting, which followed in the footsteps of an important roundtable discussion on Latin American feminist anthropologies that was held at the International Union of Anthropological and Ethnological Sciences (IUAES) 2021 Congress. Topics discussed included definitions of feminist anthropology, feminist anthropological genealogies, the feminist anthropological canon, the contributions of feminist anthropology, the relationship between feminist scholarship and feminist activism, and the major theoretical, ethnographic, political, ethical, methodological, topical, and pedagogical challenges facing feminist anthropology and feminist anthropologists globally today. Participants included members of the Association for Feminist Anthropology section of the AAA, the IUAES Commission on Global Feminisms and Queer Politics, and the Society for Applied Anthropology Gender‐Based Violence Topical Interest Group.

items.title: Between Secrecy and Ostentation: Shrines and Rites for the Barbarous Relic
items.affiliation: Banque de France; Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Central bank gold vaults occupy a paradoxical position in contemporary monetary systems: They are among the most symbolically charged and institutionally significant spaces of modern finance, yet they have received almost no scholarly attention. This article argues that gold vaults cannot be understood solely as technical infrastructures for the safekeeping of bullion. Rather, they are hybrid spaces that oscillate between secrecy and ostentation, fortress and shrine, rational security apparatus and ritual site. Drawing on historical analysis, semiotics, and anthropological theories of value, I show how vaults materialize political imaginaries of sovereignty, embody cosmologies of value, and perform ritual functions that anchor collective belief in monetary order. The first part traces the evolution of vault architecture in France, the United Kingdom, Spain, and the United States, demonstrating how their militarization responded to shifting geopolitical and technological threats while simultaneously projecting state power. The second part examines the latent ritual and apotropaic dimensions of vaults in the post–Bretton Woods era, when gold's monetary role diminished even as its symbolic potency intensified. By foregrounding the dual nature of vaults as both defensive infrastructures and sacred repositories, the article reveals how these spaces help produce confidence, authenticate value, and sustain the mythic foundations of contemporary capitalism.
